 pronounced/passed the following:
 Order

This petition under Section 482 of the Cr.P.C. has been filed by the petitioner seeking the quashment of the order dated 23.08.2023 passed in Cr.R. No.277/2023, whereby the revision filed by the petitioner was dismissed and the order dated 05.08.2023 passed in RCT No.854/2015 was upheld.
The Petitioner also seeks quashment of FIR bearing crime No.578/2014 and all consequential proceedings.

2. The facts of the case are that the complainant, who is the brother-in- law of the Petitioner, lodged the impugned FIR No.578/2014 on 18/09/2014, alleging that a cheque of Rs.32,37,800/- was fraudulently encashed by the Petitioner.

The complainant further alleged that the cheque book NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2025:MPHC-GWL:31281 2 MCRC-41396-2023 containing blank signed cheques went missing in December, 2010, and later, one such cheque was allegedly misused by the Petitioner.

The charges framed under Section 420 IPC were quashed by the High Court in M.Cr.C.

sentences.text: 1 Magistrate on 05.08.2023 passed an order of committal to the Sessions Court, holding that a prima facie case for Section 403 and 467 of IPC was made out, against which, the Petitioner filed a revision petition before the learned Revisional Court, which was rejected on 23.08.2023, on the grounds that the order of committal was interlocutory and no legal error had occurred.
Being aggrieved by the impugned orders Annexure P/1 & P/2 as well as the FIR bearing No. 578/2014 the present petition is being filed.
3. Learned counsel for the petitioner submits that the impugned order is unsustainable, as the revision was maintainable and the order in question is not interlocutory in nature.

It is further submitted that since the petition under Section 138 of the NI Act has already been dismissed by this Court, the statutory presumptions under Sections 118 and 139 of the NI Act operate in favour of the petitioner, and no offence under Sections 403 or 463/467 IPC is made out against him.
The bank transactions and admitted signatures clearly establish that the cheque was issued towards a legally enforceable debt; hence, the FIR and the committal order are ex facie illegal.
It is argued that the alleged complaint regarding loss of the cheque book is forged, as no such record exists in the concerned police station.

Proceedings under Section 209 NEUTRAL CITATION NO.
2025:MPHC-GWL:31281 3 MCRC-41396-2023 CrPC are not interlocutory in nature, and therefore the denial of a revisional remedy is erroneous.
The court below further committed an error in declaring the revision non-maintainable while simultaneously recording findings on merits.
It is urged that a cheque-bounce case is already pending against the complainant.
After the cheque was dishonoured and statutory notice issued, the complainant falsely concocted a story of the cheque having been lost.
The relationship between the parties; complainant being the petitioner's brother-in-law, has been concealed.
The complainant has admitted signing the cheque, which itself negates any offence under Sections 403 or 467 IPC.
Once the signatures are admitted, mere allegations of misuse cannot justify committal; both courts below have misinterpreted Section 403 IPC.

The complainant's versions are mutually contradictory; initially alleging loss of a blank cheque book, thereafter claiming that only one signed cheque was lost, and later presenting yet another inconsistent version before the court, thus no prima facie case is made out.
Even assuming the revision to be non- maintainable, the present petition under Section 482 CrPC is maintainable.
The charge under Section 420 IPC already stands dismissed, and there is no material indicating cheating or conspiracy.
The statutory presumption under Section 139 NI Act has not been rebutted, rendering findings under Sections 403 and 467 IPC unsustainable.
It is submitted that permitting such complaints would amount to an abuse of the process of law, enabling defaulters to escape liability by falsely claiming loss of cheques.

On these grounds, it is humbly prayed that this Court may be pleased to allow the present petition and quash the impugned orders as well as FIR No. 578/2014 NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2025:MPHC-GWL:31281 4 MCRC-41396-2023 and all consequential proceedings, in the interest of justice.
4. Per contra, learned counsel for the State as well as the complainant have opposed the petition and supported the impugned orders.

It is submitted that the allegations contained in the FIR disclose commission of cognizable offences, and the disputed questions raised by the petitioner cannot be adjudicated in a petition under Section 482 Cr.P.C.

It is further submitted that the complainant has specifically alleged that his signed cheque was misused by the petitioner for wrongful gain, and the material collected during investigation prima facie supports the said allegation.

sentences.text: Having considered the submissions of both the parties and perused the material on record, this Court is of the opinion that the FIR as well as the impugned orders disclose prima facie material warranting adjudication in trial.

The defence raised by the petitioner regarding presumption under the NI Act, alleged contradictions in the complainant's statements, bank transactions, and legality of the cheque issuance, all involve disputed questions of fact which cannot be examined in proceedings under Section 482 Cr.P.C.
The committal order passed by the learned Magistrate and affirmed by the Revisional Court does not suffer from illegality or perversity.
Furthermore, the Revisional Court rightly held that the revision was not maintainable against an interlocutory order.
Hence, this Court finds no ground to exercise inherent jurisdiction under Section 482 Cr.P.C. for quashing the FIR or the consequential proceedings.
6. Accordingly, the present petition under Section 482 Cr.P.C. stands dismissed.
